title: Research Bite 84 Retrieval Spacing and Interleaving in Real Classrooms 9, 2026
author: Craig Barton
source: Tips for Teachers newsletter (tipsforteachers.substack.com), on Ruitenburg et al., November
summary: In Research Bite 84, Craig Barton breaks down a meta-analysis by Sterre Ruitenburg and colleagues that pooled 53 studies and 7,303 students aged 6 to 18 to test retrieval practice, spaced practice and interleaving in authentic school classrooms. All three strategies improved learning, with average effect sizes of 0.37 for retrieval, 0.20 for spacing and 0.40 for interleaving, smaller than lab findings but large for school interventions. Barton draws out when each works: retrieval for factual knowledge and when practice matches the test format, spacing when gaps run between a tenth and the whole of the time to the test, and interleaving when feedback is delayed or absent. He warns that findings about boundary conditions rest on few studies and that only two came from the UK. The practical advice is to build understanding first, mirror the final assessment, space practice sensibly, and hold answers back on mixed problem sets.
points: Retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving all work in real classrooms, but with smaller effects than lab studies suggest, so expect solid rather than spectacular gains.
Retrieval practice secures factual knowledge but did not reliably help conceptual understanding, so teach for understanding first and then quiz to keep the underlying facts secure.
Match practice questions to the format of the final test, because retrieval worked better when practice and assessment used the same question type.
Space practice with gaps between about a tenth and the whole of the time until the test, rather than on consecutive days.
Interleaved problem sets worked when students received no immediate answers, so give feedback after the session instead of after each question.
quotes: Retrieval practice, spaced practice and interleaving are widely recommended to schools, but most of the evidence behind them comes from labs and universities.

All three strategies improved learning, with average effect sizes of 0.37 for retrieval practice, 0.20 for spacing and 0.40 for interleaving. These are smaller than lab-based reviews have found, but large by the standards of school interventions.
Their explanation is that recalling information strengthens memory of material students already understand, so the understanding has to be built beforehand.
If students will need to write a definition from memory in the exam, quizzing them only with multiple-choice questions may not prepare them well.
So if an end-of-unit test is four weeks away, leave somewhere between three days and four weeks between practice sessions on a topic, instead of practising it on consecutive days.
The authors suggest that instant answers remove the need to work out which method each problem calls for, which is the skill interleaving is meant to build.
The interleaving evidence is thin (ten studies, mostly maths), and only two of the 53 studies came from the UK.
